newsitem.title: FRANCE: Guatemalan president, rebel share U.N. peace prize.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan president, rebel share U.N. peace prize.

text.p: UNESCO awarded its 1996 peace prize on Wednesday to Guatemalan President Alvaro Arzu and rebel leader Rolando Moran for signing an agreement ending decades of bloodshed in the Central American state.

The Felix Houphouet-Boigny peace prize, awarded annually by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation is worth 800,000 francs ($145,000), to be shared between the two men, a UNESCO spokewoman said.

"Our jury decided what is an unprecedented step of honouring both the government, the president of Guatemala, as well as the head of the guerrilla movement who with international sanction agreed to end their civil war," said former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, president of the jury which met at UNESCO's Paris headquarters.
Some 140,000 people were killed or "disappeared" during the 36-year conflict, most of them in the Cold War years of the 1980s, before the peace accord was signed on December 29.
Kissinger said civil wars and guerrilla wars were "perhaps the biggest threat to peace in the world today."

He said other conflicts which the jury considered because they had either ended or progress was made towards peace included Bosnia, Sierra Leone and the Philippines where authorities face the Moro Front.
Kissinger said the jury voiced "hope that this (Guatemala) is the model that should be followed wherever civil and ethnic conflict are causing such enormous human suffering."
The jury included former Portugese President Mario Soares and ex-Colombian president Misael Pastrana Borrero as well as ex-cabinet ministers from France and Senegal.

The award, sometimes called the "little Nobel" because it is awarded several months before the more prestigious Nobel prize, is named after the long-serving first president of Ivory Coast, who died in 1993.
Its first joint laureates were South Africa's then opposition leader Nelson Mandela and president Frederick De Klerk for agreeing to end apartheid.

In 1993, UNESCO was first to reward the Israeli-PLO peace agreement by giving its prize to the late Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, his foreign minister Shimon Peres and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat. They later won the Nobel peace prize.
The 1995 prize went to U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata of Japan.
